name: Suryanar Kovil
deity: Surya (Suryanar), with consorts Ushadevi and Pratyusha Devi
significance: The one Navagraha temple of Tamil Nadu whose principal shrine belongs to the Sun rather than to Shiva, raised under Kulothunga Chola I as the Kulottungachola-Marttandalaya and enlarged in the Vijayanagara period. It carries a five-tiered rajagopuram and is now run by the state Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.
story: Legend holds that the nine planetary deities, struck with leprosy by Brahma's curse and banished to Vellurukku Vanam, were allowed by Shiva to bless devotees from this spot.

name: Kailasanathar Temple, Thingalur
deity: Shiva as Kailasanathar; Navagraha shrine of Chandra (the Moon)
builtDisplay: 16th c. Nayak structure on a Chola foundation
significance: One of the nine Navagraha temples of Tamil Nadu, assigned to the Moon, standing between Thanjavur and Kumbakonam. The site is praised in the 7th-century Tevaram as a Vaippu Sthalam, and its present masonry was built by the Nayaks over an earlier Chola complex.
story: The moon god Chandra is said to have worshipped Kailasanathar here after a curse dimmed him, and to have regained his powers in return.

name: Nagannathaswamy Temple, Keelaperumpallam
deity: Shiva as Naganatha Swamy; Navagraha shrine of Ketu
builtDisplay: 16th c. Nayak structure on a Chola foundation
significance: Known as the Ketu Sthalam, this is the Navagraha temple of Tamil Nadu tied to the shadow planet Ketu, about two kilometres from Poompuhar in Mayiladuthurai district. A flat rajagopuram and two prakarams enclose the Nayak-period masonry raised over a Chola foundation.
story: After the churning of the ocean of milk loosed the poison Halahala, the serpent Vasuki is said to have prayed here and Shiva appeared as Naganathar to grant redemption.

name: Sri Lakshmi Narayani Golden Temple (Sripuram)
significance: A modern gold-sheathed shrine at Thirumalaikodi near Vellore, completed in August 2007 by the Sri Narayani Peedam trust led by Sakthi Amma. It sits on about forty hectares of the Thirupuram spiritual park and is approached along a star-shaped Sri Chakra path more than 1.8 km long.

name: Vadapalani Andavar Temple
significance: A major Murugan shrine in western Chennai that began in 1865 as a thatched hut where Annaswami Nayakar worshipped a painted image of the god, with the masonry temple following around 1890 and renovation in 1920. Its rajagopuram carries stucco panels of episodes from the Skanda Purana.
story: A sage of Palani is said to have appeared in Annaswami Nayakar's dream and told him to worship Murugan at home, which is how the shrine began.

name: Ashtalakshmi Temple, Chennai
deity: Lakshmi in her eight forms (Ashta Lakshmi)
significance: A seaside temple at Besant Nagar begun in 1974 and consecrated in April 1976 at the wish of the Kanchi seer Chandrashekarendra Saraswati. Modelled on the Sundara Varadaraja Perumal temple at Uthiramerur, it stacks nine sanctums across four levels so pilgrims can visit every shrine without walking above another sanctum.

name: Adhiparasakthi Siddhar Peetam, Melmaruvathur
significance: A goddess shrine on the Chennai–Tiruvannamalai road that grew around a swayambhu stone exposed when a storm uprooted a neem tree in 1966. Villagers first raised a hut over the stone, and the image of Adi Parashakti was installed in November 1977.
story: The neem tree that stood here is said to have dripped a healing nectar, and the Mother is believed to dwell in the snake mound as a cobra so as to keep blessing devotees.

name: Sittanavasal Cave
builtDisplay: 7th c. Pandya renovation; ascetic use from c. 2nd c. BCE
significance: A rock-cut Jain monastery and cave temple in Pudukkottai district, used by Shramana ascetics from about the 2nd century BCE. An inscription credits its renovation to a Pandya king of the 7th century, and the Archaeological Survey of India now maintains it as a ticketed monument.

name: Kalugumalai Jain Beds
deity: Jain Tirthankaras, including Parshvanatha and Gomateshwara
significance: About 150 rock-cut niches of Tirthankaras carved into the Kalugumalai hill under the Pandya king Parantaka Nedunjadaiya in the late 8th century, left unfinished. Its 98 inscriptions form the largest single concentration of Jain epigraphs in the far south, a fifth of them naming women mendicants.

name: Ranganathaswamy Temple, Srirangapatna
dynasty: Western Ganga, with Hoysala and Vijayanagara additions
significance: The upstream shrine of the three Ranganatha temples on the Kaveri, recorded by inscription as founded in 894 CE by the chief Tirumalaiah under Western Ganga rule. It was enlarged by the Hoysalas under Vishnuvardhana, renovated in 1210 under Veera Ballala II, and extended again in the Vijayanagara and Wodeyar periods.

name: Satyanarayana Swamy Temple, Annavaram
significance: A hilltop shrine on Ratnagiri in Kakinada district, first built in 1891 and rebuilt in stone in 1933–34. It is one of the busiest pilgrimage centres in Andhra Pradesh, visited above all for the collective performance of the Satyanarayana Vratam, especially in the month of Karthika.
story: The hill is said to be a son of the mountain Meru and his wife Menaka, blessed by Vishnu, on whom Satyanarayana chose to manifest.

name: Dwaraka Tirumala Temple
significance: A Venkateswara temple in Eluru district that draws pilgrims from across coastal Andhra and is known locally as Chinna Tirupati, or little Tirupati.

name: Varasidhi Vinayaka Swamy Temple, Kanipakam
significance: A Ganesha temple in Chittoor district built in the early 11th century under the Chola emperor Kulottunga I and expanded in 1336 under the Vijayanagara rulers. The image stands in a well that never runs dry and is administered today by the Andhra Pradesh endowments department through a trust board.
story: Three disabled brothers digging a well are said to have struck a hard object from which blood gushed; they were healed on the spot, and the self-manifested Ganesha has stayed in the water ever since, the image reportedly growing so that its old silver armour no longer fits.

name: Srikurmam Temple
deity: Vishnu as Kurmanatha, the tortoise avatar
significance: One of very few temples in India where Vishnu is worshipped in his Kurma or tortoise form. A temple inscription of 1281 CE records the restoration of Kurmakshetra by Ramanuja under the Eastern Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva, and the complex carries inscriptions running from the 11th to the 19th century.

name: Arasavalli Sun Temple
dynasty: Eastern Ganga; rebuilt in the 18th c.
significance: One of the very few Indian temples where Surya remains the presiding deity, founded in the 7th century under the Eastern Ganga king Devendra Varma a kilometre east of Srikakulam. The building standing today is largely the result of 18th-century work, reconstructed in 1778 by Elamanchili Pullaji Panthulu.
story: The Padma Purana holds that the sage Kasyapa installed the image of Surya here for the welfare of mankind.

name: Madhukeswara Temple, Mukhalingam
significance: The principal Shaiva temple of Mukhalingam, the town that served as Kalinganagari, capital of the Eastern Gangas, and built under Kamarnava Deva II around the turn of the 9th century. Two further Shaiva temples stand in the village, the latest dating to the early 11th century, and the group was renovated by the Maharaja of Paralakhemundi in the 17th century.

name: Yaganti Uma Maheswara Temple
deity: Shiva with Parvati as Uma Maheswara
significance: A hill temple in Nandyal district built in the 15th century by Harihara Bukka Raya of the Sangama dynasty of Vijayanagara, where Shiva and Parvati are worshipped together as Uma Maheswara. Its pushkarini is fed through a carved bull, and the hillside holds the Agastya, Venkateswara and Veera Brahmam caves.
story: Tradition says the sage Agastya meant to raise a Venkateswara temple here, but the image's toe broke, so he did penance and Shiva granted the shrine instead.

name: Mahanandiswara Swamy Temple, Mahanandi
style: Badami Chalukya gopuram with Vijayanagara additions
significance: The chief shrine of the Nava Nandi group of nine Nandi temples near Nandyal, its original structure built by the Badami Chalukyas in the 7th century with further work in the 10th and 15th centuries. Tenth-century inscriptions record repairs made under the local Nanda rulers.
story: Local tradition traces the name to the Nanda rulers of the region, who worshipped Nandi as their ancestral deity.

name: Trikoteswara Swamy Temple, Kotappakonda
deity: Shiva as Trikoteswara, lord of the three peaks
significance: A three-peaked hill shrine in Palnadu district whose exact foundation date is unknown but which received land and cattle grants from the Eastern Chalukyas and Kakatiyas between the 9th and 14th centuries. Vijayanagara rulers added Dravidian mandapams and gopurams, and the temple is now administered by Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams.
story: The god is linked to Anandavalli, a cowherd woman whose fierce devotion is said to have drawn Shiva from Rudra Shikharam to Brahma Shikharam, where he settled as the lingam of the present temple.

name: Amaralingeswara Temple, Amaravati
deity: Shiva as Amareswara, with Bala Chamundika
dynasty: Kota chiefs, with Reddi and Vijayanagara patronage
significance: One of the five Pancharama Kshetras, standing above the Krishna at Amaravati around a white marble lingam some fifteen feet tall. Its earliest inscription dates to 1129 CE, and it drew patronage from the Kota chiefs, the Reddi kings, Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara and, in the late 18th century, Vasireddy Venkatadri Nayudu.
story: The gods are said to have settled at this spot after Shiva vowed to destroy the demon king Tarakasura, which is why the place is called Amaravati, the abode of the immortals.

name: Bhimeswara Swamy Temple, Draksharamam
significance: One of the five Pancharama Kshetras of Shiva, in the Konaseema district village formerly called Dakshatapovana or Dakshavatika. Eight lingas consecrated around it in the eight directions are known as the Ashta Someswaras.

name: Kumararama Bhimeswara Temple
deity: Shiva as Kumara Bhimeswara, with Bala Tripura Sundari
significance: One of the five Pancharama Kshetras, begun in 892 CE and finished by 922 under the Chalukya king Bhima, with later work by the Kakatiyas and the Musunuri Nayaks between 1340 and 1466. It holds a sixteen-foot limestone linga and a hundred-pillared mandapam, and is a centrally protected monument of national importance; inscriptions from 1147 to 1494 record its gifts and endowments.

name: Ksheerarama Temple
deity: Shiva as Ksheera Ramalingeswara Swamy, with Parvati
significance: One of the five Pancharama Kshetras sacred to Shiva, built at Palakollu during the Chalukya period in the 9th century under Chalukya Bhima. Its prakara was laid out in the 10th century by Sri Velupathi and its gopuram raised in the 14th under Alladu Reddy, with a kalyana mantapam and a Lakshmi Narayana shrine added in the 17th century.

name: Somarama Temple
deity: Shiva as Someswara Swamy, with Rajarajeswari
significance: One of the five Pancharama Kshetras, at Bhimavaram in West Godavari district, and a centrally protected monument of national importance. Its lotus-covered tank, the Chandrakundam, adjoins a Nandi hall and sanctum whose linga is reported to change colour with the phases of the moon.
story: The linga is said to have been installed by the moon god Chandra, which is why it turns white at the full moon and dark at the new.

name: Amaravati Stupa
dynasty: Satavahana, with earlier Sada and post-Mauryan phases
significance: A great stupa on the Krishna, perhaps 73 metres tall at its height, raised in phases from the 3rd century BCE to about 250 CE and decorated in the Amaravati school of relief sculpture ranked beside Mathura and Gandhara. Abandoned as Buddhism declined, it was rediscovered by Colin Mackenzie in 1797 and stripped of much of its sculpture by 19th-century excavators.

name: Nagarjunakonda
deity: Buddhist monastic complex, with Hindu shrines to Shiva, Kartikeya and Devi
significance: A valley of more than thirty Buddhist viharas, stupas and chaityas that flourished in the 3rd century CE when the Ikshvaku king Vashishthiputra Chamtamula made Vijayapuri his capital, with later building under the Vengi Chalukyas and the Reddi rulers. Excavated between 1954 and 1960 and then flooded by the Nagarjuna Sagar reservoir, its remains were moved to an island museum opened in 1966.

name: Undavalli Caves
significance: A four-storey rock-cut complex carved from a sandstone hill southwest of Vijayawada in the 4th and 5th centuries, chiefly under the Vishnukundinas. Used in turn as Jain quarters, a Buddhist vihara and a Hindu temple, its second floor holds a five-metre reclining Vishnu, and it is a centrally protected monument of national importance.

name: Raja Rajeswara Temple, Vemulawada
significance: A Shiva temple built between about 760 and 973 CE, when Vemulawada was the capital of the Chalukyas of Vemulawada, who ruled across what is now Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Maharashtra. It is widely called Dakshina Kashi, the Kashi of the south.

name: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Yadagirigutta
deity: Narasimha with Lakshmi, worshipped in five forms
significance: A hilltop Narasimha shrine about 65 km from Hyderabad where the god is worshipped as Jvala, Gandabherunda, Yogananda, Ugra and Lakshmi Narasimha. Long a regional pilgrimage centre supported even by the seventh Nizam, it was demolished and rebuilt entirely in stone between 2016 and 2022 on Agama and shilpa principles.
story: The Skanda Purana relates that Yada, son of the sage Rishyasringa, did penance on this hill and Narasimha appeared to him in five forms.

name: Thousand Pillar Temple
significance: A star-plan temple at Hanamkonda ordered by the Kakatiya king Rudra Deva, with three shrines under one roof for Shiva, Vishnu and Surya and a pillared hall that gives it its name. Desecrated during the Tughlaq invasion, it was later repaired with funds from the seventh Nizam and renovated again by the Government of India in 2004.

name: Bhadrakali Temple, Warangal
significance: A goddess temple beside a lake in Warangal, recorded as built in 625 CE by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II to mark his victory over the Vengi country. The Kakatiyas later took Bhadrakali as their family deity and the ruler Ganapati-deva had the adjoining lake dug; after long neglect the shrine was renovated in 1950.

name: Gnana Saraswati Temple, Basar
builtDisplay: 6th c. (King Bijialudu of Nandagiri); images reinstalled 17th c.
significance: One of only two major Saraswati temples in the subcontinent, the other being Sharada Peeth, standing on the bank of the Godavari at Basar in Nirmal district. The article credits its construction to the sixth-century Nandagiri king Bijialudu, with the images reinstalled by a later Nandagiri chieftain in the 17th century after invaders destroyed them.
story: Tradition holds that Maharishi Vyasa chose this spot after the Kurukshetra war, and that the name Basara comes from Vasara, the time he spent here in prayer.

name: Kaleshwara Mukteswara Swamy Temple
deity: Shiva as Kaleshwara Mukteshwara, twin lingas of Shiva and Yama
significance: A Shiva temple at Kaleshwaram in Bhupalpally district, counted among the three lingas that give Trilinga Desam its name. Its sanctum is unusual in holding two lingas on a single pedestal, identified with Shiva and with Yama, and pilgrims worship Ganesha, then Yama, then Shiva in that order.

name: Birla Mandir, Hyderabad
style: Blend of Dravidian, Rajasthani and Utkala
significance: A Venkateswara temple built by the Birla Foundation from two thousand tonnes of white marble on Naubat Pahad, the 280-foot hill from which the Mughals and Nizams once made proclamations over Hyderabad. It opened in 1976 and was inaugurated by Swami Ranganathananda of the Ramakrishna Mission; it deliberately has no bells, so as to keep the atmosphere meditative.

name: Statue of Equality (Ramanuja)
significance: A 66-metre seated figure of the philosopher Ramanuja at Muchintal on the edge of Hyderabad, built by the Chinna Jeeyar Trust for his thousandth birth anniversary and inaugurated in February 2022. Cast in 700 tonnes of panchaloha and assembled from some 1,600 shipped pieces, it is among the tallest sitting statues in the world and was laid out according to Agama and Shilpa Shastra.

name: Chilkur Balaji Temple
significance: A Venkateswara temple on the bank of Osman Sagar at Chilkur in Ranga Reddy district, dated by the article to the 14th century. It keeps no hundi and accepts no money from devotees, fought successfully to stay outside government endowment control, and is popularly called Visa Balaji for the wishes pilgrims bring to it.

name: Sri Raghavendra Swamy Matha, Mantralayam
deity: Brindavana of Raghavendra Tirtha; Moola Rama worshipped in the matha
significance: A pilgrim village on the Tungabhadra in Kurnool district that holds the brindavana, or tomb shrine, of the Dvaita saint Raghavendra Tirtha (1621–1671), together with the matha built around it. Founded in the 15th century by Vibudhendra Tirtha at Kumbakonam and descended from Madhvacharya through Jayatirtha, it is one of the three principal Madhva monasteries known as the Mathatraya.

name: Adi Shankara Janmabhoomi Kshetram, Kalady
deity: Adi Shankara and the goddess Saradamba
significance: The shrine on the north bank of the Periyar at the village held to be Adi Shankara's birthplace, dedicated to him and to Saradamba, the presiding goddess of Sringeri. It also holds the samadhi of Shankara's mother, and has been run by the Sringeri Matha since the Raja of Travancore acquired the family property in 1905 and handed it over.
